target: Agent 1’s claim that dissection specimens are mostly already-dead animals and do not mainly involve live animals.
objection: Most dissection animals are said to be caught in the wild, and wild capture requires collecting them while they are still alive; therefore dissection programs do involve live-animal acquisition.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that if specimens are already dead, dissection sourcing is not ethically or environmentally problematic.
objection: Even if some specimens are obtained after death, wild-catching can still harm local populations and biodiversity, making the sourcing environmentally harmful and ethically unacceptable.

target: Agent 1’s claim that dissection is necessary for education because there are no adequate alternatives.
objection: Animal dissection is not required by AP Biology or the Next Generation Science Standards, and U.S. or Canadian medical schools do not use animals for physician training, so education goals can be met without it.

target: Agent 1’s claim that real dissection offers uniquely strong learning benefits.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach equally well or better than real dissections, so alternatives can achieve the same learning outcomes.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection programs primarily use live-captured animals rather than already-dead specimens.
objection: Over 98% of dissected animals were already deceased, and fetal pigs used for dissection are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills; therefore classroom dissection typically relies on already-dead specimens rather than live capture.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection animal sourcing is the relevant example of live-animal use.
objection: If specimens are already dead when obtained, then dissection programs do not primarily depend on collecting animals while alive, so the claim that live animals are used in the relevant programs is unsupported.

target: Agent 1’s claim that classroom dissection is mainly based on already-dead byproducts and not live capture.
objection: The figure that 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, together with the fact that wild capture requires living animals, implies that most specimens are not already dead when obtained for dissection.

target: Agent 1’s claim that byproduct sourcing avoids the live-capture problem.
objection: If most dissection specimens are obtained while the animals are alive, then dissection depends on live capture rather than mainly on already-dead carcasses or byproducts.

target: Agent 1’s ethical defense of dissection based on the idea that it uses dead byproducts.
objection: Wild-catching reduces local populations and biodiversity, so specimen sourcing still contributes to environmental harm and is ethically unacceptable when combined with inhumane animal treatment.

target: Agent 1’s claim that dissection should continue because it is educationally useful.
objection: If a practice is ethically unacceptable and effective non-animal alternatives exist, it should not be required in education, even if it has some instructional value.

target: Agent 2’s argument that dissection is inhumane and environmentally harmful because it uses live animals.
objection: Fetal pigs used for dissection are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, so classroom dissection can use already-slaughtered material and may reduce landfill waste rather than require additional killing.

target: Agent 2’s claim that landfill-waste framing does not excuse dissection’s ethics.
objection: If a practice does not require additional killing and reduces landfill waste, then it is not both inhumane and environmentally harmful on the grounds claimed.

target: Agent 2’s claim that alternatives fully replace the learning value of dissection.
objection: Synthetic models and simulations are substitutes for real tissue and generally do not provide the same tactile cutting, handling, or real-biological-variability experience as dissecting actual specimens.

target: Agent 2’s claim that alternatives can teach as well or better than dissection.
objection: The relevant benefits of dissection include hands-on manipulation of real tissues, visual interpretation of real anatomy, and the fine-motor and critical-thinking skills that come with those activities; alternatives do not fully reproduce those learning goals.

target: Agent 1’s claim that alternatives do not provide equivalent hands-on learning.
objection: Peer-reviewed research and educational reviews report that virtual dissection and simulation tools can produce similar performance to real dissections on anatomy assessments, including identification, conceptual understanding, and retention.

target: Agent 1’s claim that synthetic alternatives lack tactile handling and anatomical variability.
objection: Some synthetic alternatives, such as 3D-printed anatomical models and silicone organs, are designed for hands-on manipulation and can be produced in multiple variants, so they can provide both tactile experience and variability.

target: Agent 2’s general claim that dissection lacks substantial educational value.
objection: Dissection gives students direct hands-on experience with real anatomical structures, supports fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination, and creates concrete learning opportunities rather than only abstract observation.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection does not develop the skills associated with handling real specimens.
objection: Because students must manipulate specimens and interpret anatomical features directly, dissection helps build fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and critical thinking.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection does not motivate students toward science careers.
objection: Working with real specimens can create motivating “aha moments” that increase interest in science and encourage students to pursue science careers.

target: Agent 1’s overall conclusion that dissection should be part of biology education because of its benefits.
objection: Since dissection causes avoidable ethical/environmental harms, is not required for school or medical training goals, and has effective alternatives, students should not be required to dissect animals.

target: Agent 2’s claim that the live-capture critique applies to typical classroom dissection supply.
objection: Classroom dissection typically relies on already-deceased animals, including slaughter/byproduct animals like fetal pigs, so it does not primarily depend on wild-captured specimens.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection increases harm because it requires live capture.
objection: If dissection uses already-existing slaughter/byproduct animals, then it can repurpose material that would otherwise go to landfills instead of adding new harm by requiring extra killing.

target: Agent 2’s claim that synthetic alternatives fully match the relevant learning experience.
objection: Non-animal alternatives do not fully replicate the distinctive tactile and real-specimen learning components that dissection provides.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection does not encourage science careers.
objection: Hands-on dissection can create motivating experiences that increase students’ interest in science careers.

target: Agent 1’s claim that dissection is harmless if specimens are byproducts rather than wild-caught animals.
objection: Even when dissection specimens are meat-industry byproducts, classroom dissection still relies on an animal-exploitation supply chain and sustains demand for animal bodies, so it remains tied to ongoing exploitation.

target: Agent 1’s claim that byproducts remove the ethical problem.
objection: A practice that still depends on animal exploitation is ethically unacceptable even if the specimens are byproducts, especially when effective non-animal alternatives can achieve the same learning objectives.

target: Agent 1’s claim that dissection is necessary because school standards require it.
objection: AP Biology and the Next Generation Science Standards do not require animal dissection to meet biology learning goals, so dissection is not necessary to satisfy the curriculum.

target: Agent 1’s claim that students need dissection because alternatives are inadequate.
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach the relevant anatomy and biology objectives equally well or better, so effective alternatives are available.

target: Agent 1’s claim that dissection should remain required if it is not strictly necessary.
objection: If a practice is unnecessary for required learning goals and effective alternatives exist, it should not be required in education.

target: Agent 1’s claim that byproduct status makes the landfill framing ethically exculpatory.
objection: The main environmental and ethical harms occur upstream in the animal-production and killing process, so the fact that the specimens would otherwise go to landfills does not erase the underlying harms.

target: Agent 1’s claim that byproduct use means dissection avoids ethical or environmental costs.
objection: Because dissection still involves an exploitative supply chain and effective alternatives exist, the practice remains environmentally and ethically problematic and should not be required.
